## Part 1. Sparse high-dimensional linear regression

I will use the standard high-dimensional assumptions: rows of \(X\) are sub-Gaussian, columns are normalized so that \(n^{-1}\|X_j\|_2^2 \asymp 1\), \(\Sigma\) has bounded eigenvalues on sparse directions, and a restricted eigenvalue/compatibility condition holds for sparsity level \(k\). Constants below may depend on those design constants but not on \(n,p,k\). Let

\[
\widehat \Sigma=\frac1n X^\top X,\qquad S=\{j:\beta_j\neq 0\},\qquad |S|\le k.
\]

---

### Part 1a. Lasso and its rates

The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat \beta
=
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda \|b\|_1
\right\}.
\]

The tuning parameter is chosen of the order

\[
\lambda \asymp \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

more precisely, one usually takes \(\lambda\ge 2\|X^\top \varepsilon/n\|_\infty\). Under Gaussian errors and normalized columns,

\[
\|X^\top \varepsilon/n\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

so \(\lambda=C\sigma\sqrt{\log p/n}\) with \(C>0\) sufficiently large is valid.

Under the restricted eigenvalue condition, the standard Lasso rates are

\[
\frac1n\|X(\widehat\beta-\beta)\|_2^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right),
\]

and

\[
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

---

### Part 1b. Estimation of \(\sigma^2\)

A natural residual-based estimator is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2.
\]

Let

\[
\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta.
\]

Since \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\),

\[
y-X\widehat\beta
=
\varepsilon-X\Delta.
\]

Therefore

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon-X\Delta\|_2^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
-
\frac2n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta
+
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\sigma^2-\sigma^2
=
\left(\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2-\sigma^2\right)
-
2\left(\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right)
+
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2.
\]

We bound the three terms separately.

First, since \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\),

\[
\frac1{\sigma^2}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2\sim \chi_n^2,
\]

so

\[
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2-\sigma^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]

Second,

\[
\left|\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right|
\le
\left\|\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

On the usual Lasso event,

\[
\left\|\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and from Part 1a,

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\left|\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Third, again from Part 1a,

\[
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Combining,

\[
\boxed{
|\widehat\sigma^2-\sigma^2|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma^2\left\{\frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac{k\log p}{n}\right\}
\right).
}
\]

In particular, if \(k\log p/n\to 0\), then \(\widehat\sigma^2\to_{\mathbb P}\sigma^2\).

---

### Part 1c. Debiased estimator of \(\beta_1\)

The Lasso is biased because of the \(\ell_1\)-penalty. To debias \(\widehat\beta_1\), we need an approximate inverse of the first column/row of \(\widehat\Sigma\).

A standard construction is the nodewise Lasso.

Let \(X_1\in\mathbb R^n\) be the first column of \(X\), and let \(X_{-1}\) be the remaining \(p-1\) columns. Regress \(X_1\) on \(X_{-1}\) by Lasso:

\[
\widehat\gamma_1
=
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\|X_1-X_{-1}\gamma\|_2^2
+
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}\|\gamma\|_1
\right\},
\]

with

\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}
\asymp
\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Define the nodewise residual

\[
\widehat r_1
=
X_1-X_{-1}\widehat\gamma_1,
\]

and

\[
\widehat \tau_1^2
=
\frac1n\|\widehat r_1\|_2^2
+
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}\|\widehat\gamma_1\|_1.
\]

Define the vector \(\widehat m_1\in\mathbb R^p\) by

\[
\widehat m_1
=
\frac1{\widehat\tau_1^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-\widehat\gamma_1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The KKT conditions for the nodewise Lasso imply

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
\lesssim
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}},
\]

so \(\widehat m_1\) acts as an approximate first column of \(\Sigma^{-1}\).

The debiased estimator of \(\beta_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top \frac1n X^\top (y-X\widehat\beta).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\frac1n\widehat m_1^\top X^\top (y-X\widehat\beta).
\]

---

### Part 1d. Asymptotic normality and confidence interval

We prove the expansion.

Let \(\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta\). Since

\[
y-X\widehat\beta
=
X\beta+\varepsilon-X\widehat\beta
=
\varepsilon-X\Delta,
\]

we have

\[
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top(\varepsilon-X\Delta).
\]

Therefore

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
-
\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \Delta.
\]

Since \(\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1=e_1^\top\Delta\),

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
+
\left(e_1^\top-\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma\right)\Delta.
\]

Thus

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\underbrace{\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon}_{\text{Gaussian leading term}}
+
\underbrace{\left(e_1-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1\right)^\top\Delta}_{\text{remainder}}.
\]

Let

\[
R_n
=
\left(e_1-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1\right)^\top\Delta.
\]

Using Hölder's inequality,

\[
|R_n|
\le
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

On the usual events,

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
|R_n|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\frac{k\log p}{n}
\right).
\]

Assume

\[
\frac{k\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0.
\]

Then

\[
\sqrt n\, R_n/\sigma=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]

Now consider the leading term. Conditional on \(X\), \(\widehat m_1\) is fixed and

\[
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\mid X
\sim
N\left(
0,
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1
\right).
\]

Define

\[
\widehat v_1
=
\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
=
\frac{
\sqrt n\,\widehat m_1^\top X^\top\varepsilon/n
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
+
o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]

The first term is exactly \(N(0,1)\) conditional on \(X\). Therefore, by Slutsky's theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
\]

Using \(\widehat\sigma\) from Part 1b and \(\widehat\sigma/\sigma\to_{\mathbb P}1\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
\]

Thus an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widetilde\beta_1
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat v_1}{n}},
\;
\widetilde\beta_1
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat v_1}{n}}
\right],
}
\]

where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is the standard normal quantile.

---

### Part 1e. Support recovery by thresholding

Construct debiased estimators for all coordinates:

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\widehat m_j^\top \frac1n X^\top(y-X\widehat\beta),
\qquad j=1,\dots,p,
\]

where each \(\widehat m_j\) is obtained by the same nodewise Lasso construction. Let

\[
\widehat v_j=\widehat m_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j.
\]

Assume the uniform bounds

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j-e_j\|_\infty
\lesssim
\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

and

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}\widehat v_j\le \overline v
\]

with high probability.

For each \(j\),

\[
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
=
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
+
\left(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j\right)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta).
\]

The remainder satisfies uniformly

\[
\max_j
\left|
\left(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j\right)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\frac{k\log p}{n}
\right).
\]

If

\[
\frac{k\log p}{n}
=
o\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

then the remainder is negligible relative to \(\sqrt{\log p/n}\).

Conditional on \(X\),

\[
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\sim
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2\widehat v_j}{n}\right).
\]

By a union bound,

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}
\left|
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
\right).
\]

Choose a threshold

\[
\tau_n
=
A\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

where \(A>0\) is sufficiently large, for example

\[
A>\sqrt{2(1+a)\overline v}
\]

for some fixed \(a>0\), with a small additional margin to dominate the negligible remainder.

Define

\[
\boxed{
\widehat S
=
\left\{
j:\ |\widetilde\beta_j|>\tau_n
\right\}.
}
\]

Then with probability tending to one,

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}
|\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j|
\le
\tau_n.
\]

Hence, if \(j\notin S\), then \(\beta_j=0\), so

\[
|\widetilde\beta_j|
\le
\tau_n,
\]

and therefore \(j\notin \widehat S\). Thus

\[
\widehat S\subseteq S.
\]

On the other hand, if

\[
|\beta_j|\ge C\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
\]

with \(C>2A\sigma\) sufficiently large, then

\[
|\widetilde\beta_j|
\ge
|\beta_j|-|\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j|
>
\tau_n,
\]

so \(j\in\widehat S\). Therefore

\[
S_{\mathrm{strong}}
\subseteq \widehat S.
\]

Thus, with probability tending to one,

\[
\boxed{
S_{\mathrm{strong}}
\subseteq
\widehat S
\subseteq
S.
}
\]

---

# Part 2. Nonparametric regression and additive models

---

## Part 2a. Smoothing spline and local linear estimators

Assume \(t_i\in[0,1]\) and

\[
y_i=f(t_i)+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\mid t_i]=0.
\]

### Smoothing spline estimator

For the usual cubic smoothing spline, the estimator is

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_{f\in W_2^2[0,1]}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(t_i))^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_0^1 \{f''(t)\}^2\,dt
\right\}.
\]

More generally, for an order-\(m\) smoothing spline,

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_{f\in W_2^m[0,1]}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(t_i))^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_0^1 \{f^{(m)}(t)\}^2\,dt
\right\}.
\]

---

### Local linear estimator of \(f(x_0)\) and \(f'(x_0)\)

Let \(K\) be a kernel and \(h>0\) a bandwidth. Define

\[
K_h(u)=\frac1hK\left(\frac{u}{h}\right).
\]

The local linear estimator is obtained by solving

\[
(\widehat a,\widehat b)
=
\arg\min_{a,b\in\mathbb R}
\sum_{i=1}^n
K_h(t_i-x_0)
\left[
y_i-a-b(t_i-x_0)
\right]^2.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\widehat f(x_0)=\widehat a,
\qquad
\widehat f'(x_0)=\widehat b.
}
\]

Explicitly, let \(u_i=t_i-x_0\), \(w_i=K_h(u_i)\), and define

\[
S_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i u_i^\ell,
\qquad
T_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i u_i^\ell y_i.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat a
=
\frac{S_2T_0-S_1T_1}{S_0S_2-S_1^2},
\]

and

\[
\widehat b
=
\frac{S_0T_1-S_1T_0}{S_0S_2-S_1^2}.
\]

---

## Part 2b. Closed form of smoothing spline via basis approach

Suppose the smoothing-spline solution lies in a finite-dimensional basis

\[
f(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^q b_\ell \phi_\ell(t).
\]

Let

\[
\Phi_{i\ell}=\phi_\ell(t_i),
\qquad
\Omega_{\ell m}
=
\int_0^1 \phi_\ell''(t)\phi_m''(t)\,dt.
\]

Then the criterion becomes

\[
Q(b)
=
\frac1{2n}\|y-\Phi b\|_2^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}b^\top \Omega b.
\]

Differentiate with respect to \(b\):

\[
\nabla Q(b)
=
-\frac1n\Phi^\top(y-\Phi b)
+
\lambda \Omega b.
\]

Setting \(\nabla Q(b)=0\) gives

\[
\frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi b+\lambda \Omega b
=
\frac1n\Phi^\top y.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)b
=
\Phi^\top y.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat b
=
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)^{-1}
\Phi^\top y.
}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\widehat f(t)
=
\phi(t)^\top
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)^{-1}
\Phi^\top y,
}
\]

where \(\phi(t)=(\phi_1(t),\dots,\phi_q(t))^\top\).

For the exact natural cubic smoothing spline, the representer theorem gives a basis consisting of the null space of the penalty plus kernel functions. Namely,

\[
\widehat f(t)
=
\sum_{\nu=1}^2 d_\nu \eta_\nu(t)
+
\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K(t_i,t),
\]

where \(\eta_1(t)=1\), \(\eta_2(t)=t\), and \(K\) is the reproducing kernel associated with the penalty \(\int (f'')^2\). Let

\[
T_{i\nu}=\eta_\nu(t_i),
\qquad
K_{ij}=K(t_i,t_j).
\]

Then \((\widehat c,\widehat d)\) solve

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
K+n\lambda I_n & T\\
T^\top & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat c\\
\widehat d
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

This is the usual closed-form smoothing-spline representation.

---

## Part 2c. Sparse additive model with smooth components

Consider

\[
y_i
=
\sum_{j=1}^p f_j(X_{ij})+\varepsilon_i,
\]

with only a small subset \(S=\{j:f_j\neq 0\}\) active and each \(f_j\) smooth.

We need to impose identifiability, for example

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})=0
\]

for every \(j\), and include an intercept \(\mu\).

A natural estimator is the sparse additive model estimator:

\[
(\widehat \mu,\widehat f_1,\dots,\widehat f_p)
=
\arg\min_{\mu,\, f_j\in \mathcal H}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
y_i-\mu-\sum_{j=1}^p f_j(X_{ij})
\right]^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|f_j\|_n
+
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p J(f_j)^2
\right\},
\]

subject to

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})=0.
\]

Here

\[
\|f_j\|_n
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})^2
\right)^{1/2}
\]

is the empirical \(L_2\)-norm, and

\[
J(f_j)^2
=
\int \{f_j^{(m)}(x)\}^2\,dx
\]

is a Sobolev roughness penalty.

The penalty

\[
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|f_j\|_n
\]

is a group-Lasso-type penalty and encourages entire functions \(f_j\) to be zero, giving sparsity. The penalty

\[
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p J(f_j)^2
\]

enforces smoothness.

In practice, represent each \(f_j\) in a spline basis:

\[
f_j(x)
=
\sum_{\ell=1}^q \theta_{j\ell} B_\ell(x).
\]

Let \(B_j\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\) have entries

\[
(B_j)_{i\ell}=B_\ell(X_{ij}),
\]

after centering the columns. Let \(\theta_j=(\theta_{j1},\dots,\theta_{jq})^\top\). Then the estimator becomes

\[
\widehat \theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}
\left\|
y-\bar y\mathbf 1-\sum_{j=1}^p B_j\theta_j
\right\|_2^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\left(
\frac1n\theta_j^\top B_j^\top B_j\theta_j
\right)^{1/2}
+
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p
\theta_j^\top \Omega \theta_j
\right\},
\]

where

\[
\Omega_{\ell m}
=
\int B_\ell^{(m)}(x)B_m^{(m)}(x)\,dx.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat f_j(x)=B(x)^\top \widehat\theta_j.
\]

The estimated support is

\[
\widehat S
=
\left\{
j:\ \|\widehat f_j\|_n>0
\right\}.
\]

This estimator accounts simultaneously for sparsity through the group penalty and smoothness through the Sobolev/spline roughness penalty.

\[
\widehat \Sigma=\frac1n X^\top X,\qquad S=\{j:\beta_j\neq 0\},\qquad |S|\le k.
\]

---

### Part 1a. Lasso and its rates

The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat \beta
=
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda \|b\|_1
\right\}.
\]

The tuning parameter is chosen of the order

\[
\lambda \asymp \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

more precisely, one usually takes \(\lambda\ge 2\|X^\top \varepsilon/n\|_\infty\). Under Gaussian errors and normalized columns,

\[
\|X^\top \varepsilon/n\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

so \(\lambda=C\sigma\sqrt{\log p/n}\) with \(C>0\) sufficiently large is valid.

Under the restricted eigenvalue condition, the standard Lasso rates are

\[
\frac1n\|X(\widehat\beta-\beta)\|_2^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right),
\]

and

\[
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

---

### Part 1b. Estimation of \(\sigma^2\)

A natural residual-based estimator is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2.
\]

Let

\[
\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta.
\]

Since \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\),

\[
y-X\widehat\beta
=
\varepsilon-X\Delta.
\]

Therefore

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon-X\Delta\|_2^2
=
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
-
\frac2n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta
+
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\sigma^2-\sigma^2
=
\left(\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2-\sigma^2\right)
-
2\left(\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right)
+
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2.
\]

We bound the three terms separately.

First, since \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\),

\[
\frac1{\sigma^2}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2\sim \chi_n^2,
\]

so

\[
\frac1n\|\varepsilon\|_2^2-\sigma^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]

Second,

\[
\left|\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right|
\le
\left\|\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

On the usual Lasso event,

\[
\left\|\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and from Part 1a,

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\left|\frac1n\varepsilon^\top X\Delta\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Third, again from Part 1a,

\[
\frac1n\|X\Delta\|_2^2
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma^2\frac{k\log p}{n}\right).
\]

Combining,

\[
\boxed{
|\widehat\sigma^2-\sigma^2|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma^2\left\{\frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac{k\log p}{n}\right\}
\right).
}
\]

In particular, if \(k\log p/n\to 0\), then \(\widehat\sigma^2\to_{\mathbb P}\sigma^2\).

---

### Part 1c. Debiased estimator of \(\beta_1\)

The Lasso is biased because of the \(\ell_1\)-penalty. To debias \(\widehat\beta_1\), we need an approximate inverse of the first column/row of \(\widehat\Sigma\).

A standard construction is the nodewise Lasso.

Let \(X_1\in\mathbb R^n\) be the first column of \(X\), and let \(X_{-1}\) be the remaining \(p-1\) columns. Regress \(X_1\) on \(X_{-1}\) by Lasso:

\[
\widehat\gamma_1
=
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\|X_1-X_{-1}\gamma\|_2^2
+
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}\|\gamma\|_1
\right\},
\]

with

\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}
\asymp
\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Define the nodewise residual

\[
\widehat r_1
=
X_1-X_{-1}\widehat\gamma_1,
\]

and

\[
\widehat \tau_1^2
=
\frac1n\|\widehat r_1\|_2^2
+
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}}\|\widehat\gamma_1\|_1.
\]

Define the vector \(\widehat m_1\in\mathbb R^p\) by

\[
\widehat m_1
=
\frac1{\widehat\tau_1^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-\widehat\gamma_1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The KKT conditions for the nodewise Lasso imply

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
\lesssim
\lambda_{\mathrm{node}},
\]

so \(\widehat m_1\) acts as an approximate first column of \(\Sigma^{-1}\).

The debiased estimator of \(\beta_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top \frac1n X^\top (y-X\widehat\beta).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\frac1n\widehat m_1^\top X^\top (y-X\widehat\beta).
\]

---

### Part 1d. Asymptotic normality and confidence interval

We prove the expansion.

Let \(\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta\). Since

\[
y-X\widehat\beta
=
X\beta+\varepsilon-X\widehat\beta
=
\varepsilon-X\Delta,
\]

we have

\[
\widetilde\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top(\varepsilon-X\Delta).
\]

Therefore

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1
+
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
-
\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \Delta.
\]

Since \(\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1=e_1^\top\Delta\),

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
+
\left(e_1^\top-\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma\right)\Delta.
\]

Thus

\[
\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1
=
\underbrace{\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon}_{\text{Gaussian leading term}}
+
\underbrace{\left(e_1-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1\right)^\top\Delta}_{\text{remainder}}.
\]

Let

\[
R_n
=
\left(e_1-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1\right)^\top\Delta.
\]

Using Hölder's inequality,

\[
|R_n|
\le
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1.
\]

On the usual events,

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1-e_1\|_\infty
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(\sigma k\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
|R_n|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\frac{k\log p}{n}
\right).
\]

Assume

\[
\frac{k\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0.
\]

Then

\[
\sqrt n\, R_n/\sigma=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]

Now consider the leading term. Conditional on \(X\), \(\widehat m_1\) is fixed and

\[
\widehat m_1^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\mid X
\sim
N\left(
0,
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1
\right).
\]

Define

\[
\widehat v_1
=
\widehat m_1^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_1.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
=
\frac{
\sqrt n\,\widehat m_1^\top X^\top\varepsilon/n
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
+
o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\]

The first term is exactly \(N(0,1)\) conditional on \(X\). Therefore, by Slutsky's theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
\]

Using \(\widehat\sigma\) from Part 1b and \(\widehat\sigma/\sigma\to_{\mathbb P}1\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widetilde\beta_1-\beta_1\right)
}{
\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\widehat v_1}
}
\Rightarrow
N(0,1).
}
\]

Thus an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\widetilde\beta_1
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat v_1}{n}},
\;
\widetilde\beta_1
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat v_1}{n}}
\right],
}
\]

where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is the standard normal quantile.

---

### Part 1e. Support recovery by thresholding

Construct debiased estimators for all coordinates:

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\widehat m_j^\top \frac1n X^\top(y-X\widehat\beta),
\qquad j=1,\dots,p,
\]

where each \(\widehat m_j\) is obtained by the same nodewise Lasso construction. Let

\[
\widehat v_j=\widehat m_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j.
\]

Assume the uniform bounds

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}\|\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j-e_j\|_\infty
\lesssim
\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

and

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}\widehat v_j\le \overline v
\]

with high probability.

For each \(j\),

\[
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
=
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
+
\left(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j\right)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta).
\]

The remainder satisfies uniformly

\[
\max_j
\left|
\left(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat m_j\right)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\frac{k\log p}{n}
\right).
\]

If

\[
\frac{k\log p}{n}
=
o\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right),
\]

then the remainder is negligible relative to \(\sqrt{\log p/n}\).

Conditional on \(X\),

\[
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\sim
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2\widehat v_j}{n}\right).
\]

By a union bound,

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}
\left|
\widehat m_j^\top\frac1nX^\top\varepsilon
\right|
=
O_{\mathbb P}\left(
\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
\right).
\]

Choose a threshold

\[
\tau_n
=
A\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}},
\]

where \(A>0\) is sufficiently large, for example

\[
A>\sqrt{2(1+a)\overline v}
\]

for some fixed \(a>0\), with a small additional margin to dominate the negligible remainder.

Define

\[
\boxed{
\widehat S
=
\left\{
j:\ |\widetilde\beta_j|>\tau_n
\right\}.
}
\]

Then with probability tending to one,

\[
\max_{1\le j\le p}
|\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j|
\le
\tau_n.
\]

Hence, if \(j\notin S\), then \(\beta_j=0\), so

\[
|\widetilde\beta_j|
\le
\tau_n,
\]

and therefore \(j\notin \widehat S\). Thus

\[
\widehat S\subseteq S.
\]

On the other hand, if

\[
|\beta_j|\ge C\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}
\]

with \(C>2A\sigma\) sufficiently large, then

\[
|\widetilde\beta_j|
\ge
|\beta_j|-|\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j|
>
\tau_n,
\]

so \(j\in\widehat S\). Therefore

\[
S_{\mathrm{strong}}
\subseteq \widehat S.
\]

Thus, with probability tending to one,

\[
\boxed{
S_{\mathrm{strong}}
\subseteq
\widehat S
\subseteq
S.
}
\]

# Part 2. Nonparametric regression and additive models

---

## Part 2a. Smoothing spline and local linear estimators

Assume \(t_i\in[0,1]\) and

\[
y_i=f(t_i)+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\mid t_i]=0.
\]

### Smoothing spline estimator

For the usual cubic smoothing spline, the estimator is

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_{f\in W_2^2[0,1]}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(t_i))^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_0^1 \{f''(t)\}^2\,dt
\right\}.
\]

More generally, for an order-\(m\) smoothing spline,

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_{f\in W_2^m[0,1]}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(t_i))^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_0^1 \{f^{(m)}(t)\}^2\,dt
\right\}.
\]

---

### Local linear estimator of \(f(x_0)\) and \(f'(x_0)\)

Let \(K\) be a kernel and \(h>0\) a bandwidth. Define

\[
K_h(u)=\frac1hK\left(\frac{u}{h}\right).
\]

The local linear estimator is obtained by solving

\[
(\widehat a,\widehat b)
=
\arg\min_{a,b\in\mathbb R}
\sum_{i=1}^n
K_h(t_i-x_0)
\left[
y_i-a-b(t_i-x_0)
\right]^2.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
\widehat f(x_0)=\widehat a,
\qquad
\widehat f'(x_0)=\widehat b.
}
\]

Explicitly, let \(u_i=t_i-x_0\), \(w_i=K_h(u_i)\), and define

\[
S_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i u_i^\ell,
\qquad
T_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i u_i^\ell y_i.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat a
=
\frac{S_2T_0-S_1T_1}{S_0S_2-S_1^2},
\]

and

\[
\widehat b
=
\frac{S_0T_1-S_1T_0}{S_0S_2-S_1^2}.
\]

---

## Part 2b. Closed form of smoothing spline via basis approach

Suppose the smoothing-spline solution lies in a finite-dimensional basis

\[
f(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^q b_\ell \phi_\ell(t).
\]

Let

\[
\Phi_{i\ell}=\phi_\ell(t_i),
\qquad
\Omega_{\ell m}
=
\int_0^1 \phi_\ell''(t)\phi_m''(t)\,dt.
\]

Then the criterion becomes

\[
Q(b)
=
\frac1{2n}\|y-\Phi b\|_2^2
+
\frac{\lambda}{2}b^\top \Omega b.
\]

Differentiate with respect to \(b\):

\[
\nabla Q(b)
=
-\frac1n\Phi^\top(y-\Phi b)
+
\lambda \Omega b.
\]

Setting \(\nabla Q(b)=0\) gives

\[
\frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi b+\lambda \Omega b
=
\frac1n\Phi^\top y.
\]

Therefore

\[
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)b
=
\Phi^\top y.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat b
=
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)^{-1}
\Phi^\top y.
}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\widehat f(t)
=
\phi(t)^\top
\left(\Phi^\top\Phi+n\lambda\Omega\right)^{-1}
\Phi^\top y,
}
\]

where \(\phi(t)=(\phi_1(t),\dots,\phi_q(t))^\top\).

For the exact natural cubic smoothing spline, the representer theorem gives a basis consisting of the null space of the penalty plus kernel functions. Namely,

\[
\widehat f(t)
=
\sum_{\nu=1}^2 d_\nu \eta_\nu(t)
+
\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K(t_i,t),
\]

where \(\eta_1(t)=1\), \(\eta_2(t)=t\), and \(K\) is the reproducing kernel associated with the penalty \(\int (f'')^2\). Let

\[
T_{i\nu}=\eta_\nu(t_i),
\qquad
K_{ij}=K(t_i,t_j).
\]

Then \((\widehat c,\widehat d)\) solve

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
K+n\lambda I_n & T\\
T^\top & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat c\\
\widehat d
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

This is the usual closed-form smoothing-spline representation.

---

## Part 2c. Sparse additive model with smooth components

Consider

\[
y_i
=
\sum_{j=1}^p f_j(X_{ij})+\varepsilon_i,
\]

with only a small subset \(S=\{j:f_j\neq 0\}\) active and each \(f_j\) smooth.

We need to impose identifiability, for example

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})=0
\]

for every \(j\), and include an intercept \(\mu\).

A natural estimator is the sparse additive model estimator:

\[
(\widehat \mu,\widehat f_1,\dots,\widehat f_p)
=
\arg\min_{\mu,\, f_j\in \mathcal H}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
y_i-\mu-\sum_{j=1}^p f_j(X_{ij})
\right]^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|f_j\|_n
+
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p J(f_j)^2
\right\},
\]

subject to

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})=0.
\]

Here

\[
\|f_j\|_n
=
\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(X_{ij})^2
\right)^{1/2}
\]

is the empirical \(L_2\)-norm, and

\[
J(f_j)^2
=
\int \{f_j^{(m)}(x)\}^2\,dx
\]

is a Sobolev roughness penalty.

The penalty

\[
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p \|f_j\|_n
\]

is a group-Lasso-type penalty and encourages entire functions \(f_j\) to be zero, giving sparsity. The penalty

\[
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p J(f_j)^2
\]

enforces smoothness.

In practice, represent each \(f_j\) in a spline basis:

\[
f_j(x)
=
\sum_{\ell=1}^q \theta_{j\ell} B_\ell(x).
\]

Let \(B_j\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\) have entries

\[
(B_j)_{i\ell}=B_\ell(X_{ij}),
\]

after centering the columns. Let \(\theta_j=(\theta_{j1},\dots,\theta_{jq})^\top\). Then the estimator becomes

\[
\widehat \theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p}
\left\{
\frac1{2n}
\left\|
y-\bar y\mathbf 1-\sum_{j=1}^p B_j\theta_j
\right\|_2^2
+
\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p
\left(
\frac1n\theta_j^\top B_j^\top B_j\theta_j
\right)^{1/2}
+
\rho\sum_{j=1}^p
\theta_j^\top \Omega \theta_j
\right\},
\]

where

\[
\Omega_{\ell m}
=
\int B_\ell^{(m)}(x)B_m^{(m)}(x)\,dx.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat f_j(x)=B(x)^\top \widehat\theta_j.
\]

The estimated support is

\[
\widehat S
=
\left\{
j:\ \|\widehat f_j\|_n>0
\right\}.
\]

This estimator accounts simultaneously for sparsity through the group penalty and smoothness through the Sobolev/spline roughness penalty.
